title: Earn, save, give
hook: Wesley's sermon on money: gain all you can honestly, save all you can, give all you can

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace churches: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren who refuse to fight and answer evil with good. Your line was the peaceable way. In one small conflict, what did you do instead of striking back? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

A paycheck lands on a Friday. Before a cent of it is spent, its owner has already sorted it: rent, the car, groceries, that thing in the online cart, and maybe, if anything is left, something for somebody else. John Wesley, the preacher whose followers became the Methodists, wrote a sermon about exactly that moment. He called it The Use of Money. Preachers are sometimes expected to treat money as a danger to keep at arm's length. Wesley didn't. He told his listeners to go out and earn. Today's word: earn.

Wesley's sermon gives money three rules, in order. First, gain all you can. But honestly, and with limits. Not by work that wrecks your own health. Not by hurting your neighbor, their body, their business or their soul. Earning, for Wesley, was part of faithfulness, as long as nobody paid for it with harm. Second, save all you can. And here's the surprise: by save, Wesley didn't mean stockpile. He meant cut the waste. Don't throw money at showing off, at things bought to be admired, at feeding every craving. Saving was a way of keeping money free for something better. Third, give all you can. That's where the first two were heading the whole time. In his telling, someone who earns hard and saves hard but stops there has missed the point and only built a bigger pile. Wesley wasn't inventing this. Paul tells a reformed thief in Ephesians to work with his hands, and gives the reason: "that he may have to give to him that needeth." Earning, there, is pointed outward from the start. Paul also warns Timothy that "the love of money is the root of all evil." Notice the word: the love of it, not the money itself. Wesley's three rules are one way of keeping the money and losing the love. Earn so you have something. Save so it isn't wasted. Give, because that was what it was for.

Here's the practice: give from what you saved. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last week of spending. Find one small thing you didn't really need: a delivery fee, a second coffee, an impulse buy. Hold that amount in your mind. That's your saved money, in Wesley's sense: waste you could cut. Now ask where it could go instead. A neighbor, a food bank, a friend who's short this month, a cause you already trust. Decide, but don't rush. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart. The bell holds the time.
Earn. In Wesley's sermon, the first of three rules for money: gain all you can, honestly, without harm, so that you have something to save and to give.
Your line: give all you can. Today, take the amount you found in the practice and actually give it, before the day ends. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Methodists and other Christians still teach from Wesley's sermon The Use of Money; churches often use it in teaching on stewardship, budgeting and giving.

fork.setup: you're one of Wesley's listeners. you've earned well and saved hard, and the account is growing. what does the sermon say comes next?
fork.reveal: Wesley's third rule is give all you can. in his telling, earning and saving without giving misses the point of both.

trapdoor: what you thought: a preacher would tell you to stay away from money.
what it means: Wesley says earn honestly, cut waste, and give. the money was always headed somewhere.
what a scholar hears: 1 Timothy 6:10 blames philarguria, the love of silver, not silver itself.
recall: the Latin word for this love

notes: Wesley's sermon is paraphrased, not quoted, because the exact wording of the three rules in the printed sermon was not verified; confirm the paraphrase ('gain all you can' honestly and without hurting health or neighbor; 'save all you can' meaning avoid waste on luxury, display and gratifying desires; 'give all you can') and the sermon's number in the standard collection.
'whose followers became the Methodists' is a short summary; confirm acceptable phrasing.
'Preachers are sometimes expected to treat money as a danger' is framed as an expectation, not a claim about what preachers teach; confirm.
Ephesians 4:28 applied as 'a reformed thief': the verse addresses 'him that stole'; confirm.
Trapdoor: philarguria (φιλαργυρία), love of money, literally love of silver; confirm the gloss.
